A_target.statement: Every [[Definition:Non-Empty Set|non-empty]] subset of $\N$ has a [[Definition:Smallest Element|smallest element]].

B_source.statement:
Let $\map P n$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|propositional function]] on $\N$.
If $\map P 0$ holds and $\forall n: \map P n \implies \map P {n + 1}$, then $\map P n$ holds for all $n \in \N$.

object_map.reformulation: Recast 'S has a least element' as its contrapositive and prove the complement predicate by induction (proof by contradiction).

validity_conditions: Define P(n): no element of S is <= n. P(0) holds if 0 is not in S (else 0 is the least element); the inductive step assumes no element <= n and, if n+1 were not the least, extends to n+1.
Induction then forces P(n) for all n, i.e. S has no elements, contradicting nonemptiness.
The argument is classical (uses contradiction), pairing induction with well-ordering as logically equivalent over the naturals.
proof_plan: {{AimForCont}} that $S \subseteq \N$ is non-empty with no least element.
Let $\map P n$ be the statement: no element of $S$ is $\le n$.

If $0 \in S$ it would be least, so $\map P 0$ holds.
If $\map P n$ holds and $n + 1 \in S$, then $n + 1$ would be least, so $\map P {n + 1}$ holds.
